question.text: Why do signals, signs and markings matter, and whose direction overrules them?

answer.text: Signals, signs, and markings keep traffic orderly; cutting through a lot or field to dodge them is illegal, and a police officer's direction overrules every sign and signal.

teaching.text: Dodging a signal by cutting through a lot or field is illegal, and an officer's direction comes before any sign or signal. Remember: officer beats every signal.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Signals, signs, and markings keep traffic orderly; cutting through a lot or field to dodge them is illegal, and a police officer's direction overrules every sign and signal.

question.text: Which road users must obey traffic signals?

answer.text: Traffic signals bind drivers, motorcycle riders, bicyclists, moped riders, and pedestrians alike.

teaching.text: Bicyclists, moped riders and pedestrians follow the same signals as drivers. Remember: signals bind everyone.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Traffic signals bind drivers, motorcycle riders, bicyclists, moped riders, and pedestrians alike.

question.text: Where must you stop at a red light, and how long do you stay stopped?

answer.text: At a red light, stop fully at the stop line, or before the intersection or crosswalk where no line exists, and stay stopped while red unless a turn is allowed.

teaching.text: The stop point is the line, or before the intersection or crosswalk, even when you plan to turn on red. Remember: stop at the line.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a red light, stop fully at the stop line, or before the intersection or crosswalk where no line exists, and stay stopped while red unless a turn is allowed.

question.text: What must you do before turning right on red?

answer.text: A right turn on red needs a full stop first, then a both-ways look with the right-of-way yielded to pedestrians and traffic, watching for motorcycles, bicycles, and mopeds.

teaching.text: Stop, look both ways, yield, then turn, and watch for motorcycles, bicycles and mopeds. Remember: stop, look, yield, turn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A right turn on red needs a full stop first, then a both-ways look with the right-of-way yielded to pedestrians and traffic, watching for motorcycles, bicycles, and mopeds.

question.text: Where is a right turn on red not allowed?

answer.text: No right turn on red is allowed where No Turn on Red signs stand or where a red arrow points right.

teaching.text: Two things cancel right on red: a No Turn on Red sign and a red arrow pointing right. Remember: signs or right red arrow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: No right turn on red is allowed where No Turn on Red signs stand or where a red arrow points right.

question.text: When is a left turn on red allowed?

answer.text: A left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street after a full stop and yield, and never where signs or a red left arrow forbid it.

teaching.text: Check both streets: each must be one-way before a left turn on red is allowed. Remember: one-way onto one-way only.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A left turn on red is allowed only from a one-way street onto another one-way street after a full stop and yield, and never where signs or a red left arrow forbid it.

question.text: What conditions govern right and left turns on red?

answer.text: After a full stop and yielding to pedestrians and other traffic, a right turn on red is permitted unless a No Turn on Red sign or rightward red arrow prohibits it. A left turn on red requires a one-way street leading onto another one-way street, the same stop and yield, and no prohibiting sign or leftward red arrow.

teaching.text: After a full stop and yielding to pedestrians and other traffic, a right turn on red is permitted unless a No Turn on Red sign or rightward red arrow prohibits it. A left turn on red requires a one-way street leading onto another one-way street, the same stop and yield, and no prohibiting sign or leftward red arrow. Remember: Stop, yield, check prohibitions and streets.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: After a full stop and yielding to pedestrians and other traffic, a right turn on red is permitted unless a No Turn on Red sign or rightward red arrow prohibits it. A left turn on red requires a one-way street leading onto another one-way street, the same stop and yield, and no prohibiting sign or leftward red arrow.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Stop, yield, check prohibitions and streets

question.text: What does a steady red arrow mean in Virginia?

answer.text: A red arrow means stop and stay stopped in that direction unless Right on Red Arrow After Stop or Left on Red Arrow After Stop signs are posted; Virginia otherwise bans turns at red arrows.

teaching.text: Without a red-arrow-after-stop sign, a steady red arrow holds you in place. Remember: red arrow means stay.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A red arrow means stop and stay stopped in that direction unless Right on Red Arrow After Stop or Left on Red Arrow After Stop signs are posted; Virginia otherwise bans turns at red arrows.

question.text: Why should you check the local law before turning on red outside Virginia?

answer.text: Red-light and red-arrow turn rules differ by state, so learn the local law before turning on red outside Virginia.

teaching.text: The Virginia turn-on-red rules travel with you only as far as the state line; learn the local law elsewhere. Remember: other states, other rules.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Red-light and red-arrow turn rules differ by state, so learn the local law before turning on red outside Virginia.

question.text: What must you do at a flashing red light, and what is different at a railroad crossing?

answer.text: At a flashing red light, stop fully, yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians, and go only when clear; at a railroad crossing, always stop even with no train in sight.

teaching.text: Flashing red works like a stop sign, and a railroad crossing always means a stop. Remember: flashing red: stop, yield.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a flashing red light, stop fully, yield to oncoming vehicles and pedestrians, and go only when clear; at a railroad crossing, always stop even with no train in sight.

question.text: What must you do at a flashing red arrow?

answer.text: At a flashing red arrow, stop fully, yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, and move in the arrow direction only when clear.

teaching.text: A flashing red arrow lets you go after a full stop and yield, unlike a steady red arrow. Remember: stop, yield, then arrow.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a flashing red arrow, stop fully, yield to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, and move in the arrow direction only when clear.

question.text: When may you proceed at steady or flashing red arrows?

answer.text: A steady red arrow requires waiting unless a posted sign specifically permits that turn after stopping. A flashing red arrow requires a full stop and yielding to opposing vehicles and pedestrians; proceed in its direction only when clear.

teaching.text: A steady red arrow requires waiting unless a posted sign specifically permits that turn after stopping. A flashing red arrow requires a full stop and yielding to opposing vehicles and pedestrians; proceed in its direction only when clear. Remember: Posted exception or flashing stop-and-yield.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A steady red arrow requires waiting unless a posted sign specifically permits that turn after stopping. A flashing red arrow requires a full stop and yielding to opposing vehicles and pedestrians; proceed in its direction only when clear.

question.text: How do steady and flashing red lights differ?

answer.text: At steady red, make a full stop and wait while red continues, except for a permitted turn. At flashing red, stop fully, yield to approaching vehicles and pedestrians, and continue only after the path is clear.

teaching.text: At steady red, make a full stop and wait while red continues, except for a permitted turn. At flashing red, stop fully, yield to approaching vehicles and pedestrians, and continue only after the path is clear. Remember: Steady waits except permitted turns.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At steady red, make a full stop and wait while red continues, except for a permitted turn. At flashing red, stop fully, yield to approaching vehicles and pedestrians, and continue only after the path is clear.

question.text: What does a steady yellow light or arrow tell you to do?

answer.text: A steady yellow light or arrow warns the signal is changing: stop if you have not entered, pass through cautiously if stopping is unsafe or you are already inside, and never speed up.

teaching.text: Stop if you have not entered, continue carefully only if stopping is unsafe or you are inside, and never speed up. Remember: yellow: stop, never speed.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A steady yellow light or arrow warns the signal is changing: stop if you have not entered, pass through cautiously if stopping is unsafe or you are already inside, and never speed up.

question.text: What does a flashing yellow light mean?

answer.text: A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with caution, marking a spot with higher-than-normal hazard.

teaching.text: Flashing yellow marks a higher-hazard spot, so slow down, but no stop is required. Remember: flashing yellow, slow caution.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A flashing yellow light means slow down and proceed with caution, marking a spot with higher-than-normal hazard.

question.text: How do steady and flashing yellow signals differ?

answer.text: At a steady yellow light or arrow, stop before entering if you can do so safely. If stopping is unsafe or you are already inside, continue carefully without accelerating to beat the signal. A flashing yellow means reduce speed and proceed carefully.

teaching.text: At a steady yellow light or arrow, stop before entering if you can do so safely. If stopping is unsafe or you are already inside, continue carefully without accelerating to beat the signal. A flashing yellow means reduce speed and proceed carefully. Remember: Steady: safe stop; flashing: cautious travel.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a steady yellow light or arrow, stop before entering if you can do so safely. If stopping is unsafe or you are already inside, continue carefully without accelerating to beat the signal. A flashing yellow means reduce speed and proceed carefully.
audio_scripts.must_match_memory_hook: Steady: safe stop; flashing: cautious travel

question.text: How does a flashing red differ from a flashing yellow?

answer.text: Flashing red demands a full stop plus a yield before going, while flashing yellow demands no stop at all.

teaching.text: Red flashing means stop and yield; yellow flashing means slow down. Remember: red stops, yellow slows.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Flashing red demands a full stop plus a yield before going, while flashing yellow demands no stop at all.

question.text: How do you turn at a flashing yellow arrow?

answer.text: At a flashing yellow arrow, turn in the arrow direction when clear, yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians and checking for motorcycles, bicycles, and mopeds.

teaching.text: Yield first, then turn; no full stop is needed, unlike at a flashing red arrow. Remember: yield, then turn.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a flashing yellow arrow, turn in the arrow direction when clear, yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians and checking for motorcycles, bicycles, and mopeds.

question.text: What does a green light or arrow allow, and whom must you yield to when turning without a green arrow?

answer.text: At a green light or arrow, go only when clear; turning without a green arrow means yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, and letting any pedestrian in the street finish crossing.

teaching.text: Green means go only when clear, and a turn without an arrow means yielding to people still crossing. Remember: green still means clear.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: At a green light or arrow, go only when clear; turning without a green arrow means yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, and letting any pedestrian in the street finish crossing.

question.text: How does turning on a plain green light differ from turning on a green arrow?

answer.text: Turning on a plain green light without an arrow means yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, while a green arrow in your direction means going when clear.

teaching.text: A plain green turn waits for oncoming traffic and pedestrians; a green arrow in your direction goes when clear. Remember: plain green yields more.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turning on a plain green light without an arrow means yielding to oncoming traffic and pedestrians, while a green arrow in your direction means going when clear.

question.text: What do you do when traffic signals show no lights at all?

answer.text: When signals show no lights at all, stop and cross as at an all-way stop, unless an officer or authorized person directs traffic or portable stop signs are in use.

teaching.text: A dark signal becomes an all-way stop, unless an officer directs traffic or portable stop signs stand. Remember: dark signal, all-way stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: When signals show no lights at all, stop and cross as at an all-way stop, unless an officer or authorized person directs traffic or portable stop signs are in use.

question.text: What does a red X lane signal mean?

answer.text: Never drive in a lane marked with a red X signal.

teaching.text: The red X is the strongest lane signal: never drive in that lane. Remember: red X, never drive.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never drive in a lane marked with a red X signal.

question.text: What does a yellow X or yellow diagonal downward arrow over a lane mean?

answer.text: A yellow X or yellow diagonal downward arrow means leave that lane as soon as it is safe.

teaching.text: A yellow X asks you to leave the lane safely, not to stop in it. Remember: yellow X, leave lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A yellow X or yellow diagonal downward arrow means leave that lane as soon as it is safe.

question.text: What do a green arrow and a turn arrow over a lane allow?

answer.text: A green arrow opens its lane to driving, while a one-way or two-way turn arrow lets you enter only to turn in the arrow direction.

teaching.text: A green arrow opens the lane, while a turn arrow lets you in only to turn. Remember: green arrow opens lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A green arrow opens its lane to driving, while a one-way or two-way turn arrow lets you enter only to turn in the arrow direction.

question.text: How do the red X, yellow X and green arrow lane signals differ?

answer.text: A red X bans its lane entirely, a yellow X orders a safe exit from the lane, and a green arrow opens the lane.

teaching.text: Learn the three as a set: never, leave, open. Remember: banned, exit, open.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A red X bans its lane entirely, a yellow X orders a safe exit from the lane, and a green arrow opens the lane.

question.text: What sequence does a pedestrian hybrid beacon run through?

answer.text: A pedestrian hybrid beacon runs flashing yellow, then solid yellow, then solid double red with the walk signal while drivers must stop, then alternating flashing reds that release drivers with caution once the crosswalk clears.

teaching.text: The order is flashing yellow, solid yellow, solid double red, then alternating flashing reds. Remember: yellow, double red, flashing.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A pedestrian hybrid beacon runs flashing yellow, then solid yellow, then solid double red with the walk signal while drivers must stop, then alternating flashing reds that release drivers with caution once the crosswalk clears.

question.text: How do the beacon's solid double reds differ from its alternating flashing reds?

answer.text: Solid double reds on a pedestrian beacon hold drivers stopped with walkers crossing, while the later alternating flashing reds release drivers with caution once the crosswalk clears.

teaching.text: Solid double reds mean wait while people cross; alternating flashing reds mean go with caution once the crosswalk is clear. Remember: double red holds drivers.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Solid double reds on a pedestrian beacon hold drivers stopped with walkers crossing, while the later alternating flashing reds release drivers with caution once the crosswalk clears.

question.text: Why do a sign's color and shape matter?

answer.text: A sign's color and shape warn early: shape alone may show in heavy fog, and color reads from far off before the message does.

teaching.text: Shape can show through heavy fog and color reads from far off, so you know the kind of sign before its words. Remember: shape in fog, color far.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: A sign's color and shape warn early: shape alone may show in heavy fog, and color reads from far off before the message does.

question.text: What do red, black, yellow and yellow-green signs mean?

answer.text: Red with white means stop, yield, do not, and no; black with white carries regulatory law; yellow with black warns, with a strong yellow-green reserved for school, pedestrian, and bicyclist activity.

teaching.text: Black with white is law, yellow with black is a warning, and yellow-green marks school, pedestrian and bicyclist activity. Remember: red stops, black rules.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Red with white means stop, yield, do not, and no; black with white carries regulatory law; yellow with black warns, with a strong yellow-green reserved for school, pedestrian, and bicyclist activity.

question.text: What do black with white, yellow with black, and red with white each signal?

answer.text: Black with white states a law to obey, yellow with black warns of a hazard, and red with white orders stop, yield, or no.

teaching.text: Law in black and white, hazard in yellow and black, orders in red and white. Remember: law, hazard, stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Black with white states a law to obey, yellow with black warns of a hazard, and red with white orders stop, yield, or no.

question.text: What do green, blue, brown, orange and pink signs mean?

answer.text: Green with white gives destinations, blue with white gives motorist services, brown with white marks historic or cultural interests, orange with black warns in construction zones, and pink with black warns at incidents.

teaching.text: Orange means a construction zone and pink means an incident; green, blue and brown give information. Remember: blue services, brown history.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Green with white gives destinations, blue with white gives motorist services, brown with white marks historic or cultural interests, orange with black warns in construction zones, and pink with black warns at incidents.

question.text: How do orange and pink warning signs differ?

answer.text: Orange with black warns through construction zones, while pink with black warns at incidents.

teaching.text: Orange for work, pink for incidents, both lettered in black. Remember: orange works, pink incidents.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Orange with black warns through construction zones, while pink with black warns at incidents.

question.text: What does the eight-sided octagon mean, and who yields on ties at an all-way stop?

answer.text: The eight-sided octagon always means stop: halt fully at the sign, line, crosswalk, or curb and wait for a clear way, with every approach stopping at all-way or four-way signs and the left driver yielding on ties.

teaching.text: At an all-way stop every approach stops, and on a tie the driver on the left yields. Remember: octagon always stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The eight-sided octagon always means stop: halt fully at the sign, line, crosswalk, or curb and wait for a clear way, with every approach stopping at all-way or four-way signs and the left driver yielding on ties.

question.text: What does the triangle sign tell you to do?

answer.text: The triangle means yield: slow down, stand ready to stop, and let vehicles, pedestrians, and bicyclists pass first.

teaching.text: A yield sign asks you to slow and be ready to stop, letting vehicles, pedestrians and bicyclists go first. Remember: triangle means yield.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The triangle means yield: slow down, stand ready to stop, and let vehicles, pedestrians, and bicyclists pass first.

question.text: How does the octagon differ from the triangle?

answer.text: The eight-sided octagon always commands a full stop, while the triangle commands only slowing with a stop as needed.

teaching.text: Eight sides mean a full stop every time; three sides mean slow and stop only as needed. Remember: octagon stops, triangle slows.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: The eight-sided octagon always commands a full stop, while the triangle commands only slowing with a stop as needed.

hooks_spoken: At red, stop and wait except for a permitted turn; turning on red requires a full stop and a yield.
Left on red works only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, and Virginia bans turns at a steady red arrow unless a sign allows it.

Left on red works only from a one-way street onto another one-way street, and Virginia bans turns at a steady red arrow unless a sign allows it. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: Flashing red means a full stop and a yield before going, while flashing yellow means slow down and use caution.
Steady yellow calls for a safe stop before entry, or cautious passage if stopping is unsafe; never speed up.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of flashing and yellow signals. Flashing red means a full stop and a yield before going, while flashing yellow means slow down and use caution. Steady yellow calls for a safe stop before entry, or cautious passage if stopping is unsafe; never speed up. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: A dark signal works like an all-way stop unless an officer directs traffic or portable stop signs are used.
Red X bans the lane, yellow X means leave it safely, and a green arrow opens it.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of green, dark and lane-use signals. A dark signal works like an all-way stop unless an officer directs traffic or portable stop signs are used. Red X bans the lane, yellow X means leave it safely, and a green arrow opens it. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.

hooks_spoken: The octagon always means stop, and the triangle means slow and yield.
Orange with black warns in construction zones, and pink with black warns at incidents.
recap.narration_text: Time for a quick review of sign colors and shapes. The octagon always means stop, and the triangle means slow and yield. Orange with black warns in construction zones, and pink with black warns at incidents. Keep these ideas handy as you practice.
